big: An IPO has 10 lakh shares on offer for retail investors. 5 lakh people apply, wanting one lot each. That is far more demand than supply. Not everyone can get shares. A lottery decides.

lines: I applied and got nothing. Did I do something wrong?
Probably not. When an issue is oversubscribed, retail allotment can be by lottery. Many people receive nothing. It is normal and not a mistake.

alt: Bars showing shares applied for being four times the shares on offer
caps: The retail portion offers 10 lakh shares.
Applications come in for 40 lakh shares.
That is four times the offer, so the issue is 4 times subscribed.
Not everyone can be allotted shares, so a lottery may decide.

rows: More bids than shares on offer
Giving shares to applicants, by lottery if retail demand is large
Listing price less issue price. It can also be a loss
Retail, non-institutional and qualified institutional buyers
note: Each category has its own share of the issue.

q: An issue has 10 lakh shares on offer and receives bids for 30 lakh. What is this?
why: Undersubscribed would mean fewer bids than shares.
Bids of 30 lakh against 10 lakh on offer make it three times subscribed.
A bonus issue gives extra shares to existing holders.
A split divides shares and has no link to bids.

q: Meena applied in an oversubscribed IPO and got no shares. What is the likely reason?
opts: A lottery, and she was not picked
She made a mistake in the form
SEBI banned her from the issue
why: Retail allotment can be by lottery when demand is high.
Missing out in a lottery is not a mistake by the applicant.
A company does not pick investors by liking them.
SEBI does not ban someone for missing a lottery.

q: Rohan's IPO shares list at ₹210 against an issue price of ₹190. What is the gain per share?
why: ₹210 is the listing price, and not the gain.
₹190 is the issue price that he paid for a share.
₹400 adds the two prices, which is not how a gain works.
The gain is listing price less issue price: ₹210 less ₹190.

q: Why is a listing gain not guaranteed?
opts: Listing always lowers the price of shares
SEBI sets the listing price in advance
Shares can list below issue price
The company sets it after the listing day
why: Listing does not always lower the price either.
SEBI does not set the listing price. The market does.
Demand decides the listing price, so it can be lower than the issue price.
After listing, the market decides, and not the company.

pts: Oversubscription means more bids than shares. Retail allotment may be a lottery.
A listing gain is listing price less issue price. It can be a loss.
Missing out in a lottery is normal.
